title: Foreword
text:
📖 Condensed, interactive edition — Switch to the full verbatim manuscript →




By Jigar Shah, Co-founder SunEdison, Former Director, Loan Programs Office, U.S. Department of Energy, Co-founder Multiplier
There are moments in history when an industry reaches a turning point, not because technology failed or the markets dried up, but because the gap between ambition and execution became too costly to ignore. I believe the renewable energy industry is living through one of those moments right now. And I believe this book arrives at exactly the right time to help us close that gap.
When I founded SunEdison more than two decades ago, we were trying to solve what seemed like a financing problem. How do you get solar onto rooftops at scale when the upfront cost is prohibitive? The solar-as-a-service model unlocked a market that has since grown beyond anything we dared imagine at the time. But what I learned from that experience, and from every chapter of my career, is that the hardest part of the energy transition is never the idea. It is the relentless, disciplined work of turning that idea into a project that gets built, financed, and connected to the grid. That work happens in the land offices, the title reviews, the due diligence rooms, and the negotiating sessions with county commissions and tribal authorities.
This is Kimberlee Centera’s world. And this book is her gift to everyone who wants to succeed in it.
Over more than thirty years, Kimberlee has done the work that makes the energy transition real. Not the announcements. Not the ribbon cuttings. The work. She has guided Fortune 500 companies and independent developers through hundreds of transactions, across gigawatts of solar, wind, storage, and transmission projects, with more than $25 billion in financed value. She has seen what derails deals and what saves them. She has sat across the table from landowners who believe they control property their children already inherited. She has watched projects collapse at closing because a single signature was missing. She has navigated the mineral rights dispute nobody saw coming, the municipal road reservation buried in a decades-old title record, and the tribal artifacts mistaken for rock piles on a Wyoming site. She has done this work in good policy environments and difficult ones, and she has emerged with something rare: a clear-eyed, battle-tested understanding of what it actually takes to move a project from development to deployment.
What she has written here is not a theoretical framework. It is a field guide. It is the kind of book that could only be written by someone who has lived through the consequences of getting this work wrong, and who has built the expertise to get it right.
I want to place this book in the context of the larger challenge we face, because I think it deserves that framing.
The clean energy transition is the greatest economic transformation of our lifetimes. The opportunity is staggering in terms of investment, jobs, infrastructure, and the long-term competitiveness of the American economy. We have the technology. We have the expertise. We have, despite the policy turbulence of recent years, an enduring market logic that makes renewable energy the rational choice across an ever-expanding set of applications. For years, clean energy has been 90% of everything added to the grid, and load growth requires us to be faster.
During my time leading the Loan Programs Office within the U.S. Department of Energy I watched intelligent, well-funded teams stumble over the same categories of problems that Kimberlee addresses in these pages. Land control that hadn’t been properly verified. Ownership structures that hadn’t been fully mapped. Environmental issues that emerged too late. Mineral rights that surfaced at closing. Due diligence that had been compressed to fit a timeline rather than expanded to fit the risk. In every case, the technology worked. The economics were sound. The vision was real. What was missing was the operational discipline to bridge the gap between what a project could become and what it actually was.
I am particularly moved by Kimberlee’s attention to the human dimensions of this work, the landowners, the tribal communities, the local officials, the neighbors who live within sight of a project they may or may not have been consulted about. The energy transition is not an abstraction. It unfolds on real land, in real communities, with real stakeholders whose interests, concerns, and rights must be understood and respected. Projects that ignore this reality do not just encounter delays, they forfeit the moral authority that should accompany the work of building a cleaner world. Kimberlee understands this. Her approach to community engagement, landowner communication, and stakeholder collaboration reflects a vision of energy development that is not merely transactional but genuinely relational.
To the investors and capital allocators who will read this book: I want to speak to you directly. The clean energy investment landscape has matured enormously over the past decade, and the sophistication of the capital flowing into this sector is genuinely impressive. But capital sophistication does not automatically translate into project discipline. I have seen too many transactions where the financial engineering was impeccable, and the term sheet was structured with precision while the land agreements beneath it were shot through with risk. The message of this book is that the quality of the underlying asset determines the quality of every instrument built on top of it. Title insurance, tax equity, project finance, debt structures all rest on the foundation that Kimberlee describes. Build a strong foundation. Demand it from the developers and the teams you back. It is not overhead. It is the work.
To the developers: you are the heroes of this story, and I mean that without irony. The people who go out and identify a site, negotiate a lease, navigate a permitting process, build community support, and bring a project to financial close are performing one of the most complex and consequential acts in the modern economy. This book will make you better at it. Not because it tells you something you could not eventually learn from experience, but because it compresses decades of hard-won knowledge into a form you can actually use before you make the expensive mistakes. Read it before you acquire a project whose previous developer’s work you do not fully understand.
To the project teams, the title professionals, the environmental consultants, the legal counsel, the engineers, and every other specialist who makes up the ecosystem around a renewable energy transaction: Kimberlee has written a book that honors your work. The disciplines she describes are not support functions. They are the core of what makes this industry function. The more clearly the whole ecosystem understands that, the better the outcomes for everyone.
We are in a race. The world needs us to move faster and to do that we need to get things right the first time. In that race, execution is everything. Bankable projects are everything. The knowledge in this book is important.
Kimberlee Centera has spent thirty years acquiring that knowledge so that the rest of us can benefit from it. She has written it down with clarity, precision, and the unmistakable authority of someone who has earned every lesson the hard way.
The energy transition needs more of this. More rigor. More discipline. More willingness to do the unglamorous work that separates a project that closes from a project that doesn’t. More people who understand that vision without execution is just a press release.
This book is a call to that standard. I am proud to help introduce it to the world.

title: Introduction: Why Mergers and Acquisitions are Shaping the Renewable Energy Future
text:
Policy Changes & Immediate Effects
The renewable energy sector is evolving rapidly, with mergers and acquisitions (M&A) activities playing a pivotal role in shaping the industry’s future. This trend reflects the industry’s maturation and the increasing complexity of developing large-scale renewable projects.
Since entering the renewable energy industry over 30 years ago, I have often seen projects change ownership two or three times before reaching commercial operation. Recently, there has been an upsurge in M&A activity. The termination and restriction of certain Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) tax credits and loan guarantees is impacting renewable energy M&A activity. It has increased deal-making as companies navigate valuation pressure and look for strategic consolidations. It reshapes financing, pushing players toward more risk-hedged, structured deals. And it creates a divide between projects that locked in credits early and those now struggling under new rules.
What we are experiencing now has far-reaching implications. Among them are the following:
The “One Big Beautiful Bill” (OBBB), enacted on July 4, 2025, changes or eliminates certain tax credits that were established by the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA). It also adds Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) restrictions to remaining credits. An Executive Order directs Treasury to tighten the definition of “beginning of construction.”

title: Chapter 1: Navigating M&A Best Practices in Utility-Scale Renewable Energy Development
text:
Why Companies Prefer M&A Over Greenfield Development
Greenfield development means beginning from the ground up — site selection, permitting, financing, and construction — which can take years. Acquiring existing projects offers distinct advantages:

Time Efficiency: Expedites operational readiness by eliminating initial development phases.
Risk Mitigation: Reduces exposure to development risks like permitting delays or community opposition.
Strategic Positioning: Allows companies to quickly enter new markets or technologies.
Resource Optimization: Enables better allocation of resources by focusing on operational efficiency rather than development hurdles.

Solar projects typically require five to seven years, while wind projects can take seven to ten years — not including permitting on public lands, which can involve stakeholders such as the Bureau of Land Management or the Bureau of Indian Affairs. Securing land rights may be significantly prolonged when numerous stakeholders are engaged. M&A lets you skip the initial development phase, saving a great deal of time and risk.


M&A Projects Span a Wide Spectrum of Development Stages

Pre-construction projects possess land leases and may have obtained necessary permits; construction has not yet commenced.
Under-construction projects: Physical construction has started, reducing uncertainty around project realization.
Operational projects: Already generating energy and revenue, providing immediate cash flow.

title: Chapter 2: Verifying Land Control – The Foundation of Acquisition
text:
Critical Path Parcels
Is the land you’re getting, really your land? In the realm of renewable energy projects, land is a fundamental asset. Before finalizing any acquisition, it’s imperative to verify land control and access to ensure that the project rests on solid ground — literally and legally.
Land control is the cornerstone of every successful renewable energy project. It assures that a developer has the legal authority to enter, use, and develop a specified plot of land. Without appropriate site control, even the most promising projects might suffer major delays, legal battles, or catastrophic failure.
Developers should identify critical path parcels early in diligence — substations, transmission corridors, access routes, collector systems, and key interconnection areas. Title defects or site-control failures affecting these parcels can create disproportionate impacts on financing, construction sequencing, and COD schedules.
Renewable energy projects typically acquire property via leases, easements, or purchase agreements. Developers should work closely with title companies and ALTA surveyors to identify required Table A items and endorsement requirements early — optional survey certifications frequently become mandatory lender or title requirements during financing and closing.

title: Chapter 2: Verifying Land Control – The Foundation of Acquisition
section: Government Land Complexity and Overlapping Rights
text:
Government Land Complexity and Overlapping Rights
Developers often assume that acquiring rights from a state or local government agency will be more straightforward than negotiating with private landowners. In practice, government-owned land introduces an entirely different layer of complexity.
State trust lands, public university lands, water districts, county-owned property, and other public holdings frequently involve overlapping interests not immediately visible during preliminary diligence. A developer may secure a lease only to discover that another party retains grazing rights, farming rights, mineral interests, water access rights, or operational easements affecting the same property — and in some cases, these third-party rights can directly interfere with substations, access corridors, or interconnection infrastructure.

Checkerboard Ownership
One of the most common mistakes developers make is assuming that site control over one parcel automatically guarantees access across adjoining parcels. In many Western states, renewable energy projects cross “checkerboard” ownership patterns involving combinations of state, federal, tribal, and private land. Each parcel may carry different approval standards, title requirements, timelines, and regulatory obligations. Legal access across one tract does not necessarily establish access rights across the next.

Public vs. Private Sector Timelines
Public-sector transactions frequently operate on timelines different from private transactions. Many state and local agencies face staffing shortages, outdated systems, and increasing development volume. Even after commercial terms are negotiated, agreements may require additional review by agency counsel, governing boards, or state attorneys general before execution — minor revisions to legal descriptions, formatting, or access provisions can delay approvals for weeks or months.
Successful development on government land requires proactive communication, relationship management, and coordination across stakeholders. Experienced developers treat public-sector entities as long-term project partners rather than transactional counterparties — verifying all existing rights affecting the property, confirming legal access across adjoining tracts, prioritizing critical infrastructure parcels early, and building additional time into schedules for administrative review.

title: Chapter 2: Verifying Land Control – The Foundation of Acquisition
section: Why Land Control Matters Across the Project Lifecycle
text:
Why Land Control Matters Across the Project Lifecycle
Feasibility Studies: Land control is critical during first feasibility studies — environmental assessments and compliance review cannot proceed without site control.
Securing Financing: Lenders and investors require developers to demonstrate land control before financing can be obtained. Without it, a project is considered high-risk.
Permits and Regulatory Compliance: Zoning boards and environmental authorities may refuse to process permits unless the developer demonstrates ownership or lease rights.
Managing Risk: Acquiring land control early allows developers to proactively address ownership conflicts, title issues, or community objections before they derail the project.
Protecting Project Timelines: Renewable projects are time-sensitive, particularly with incentive schemes or financing deadlines tied to specific dates.
Failure to confirm land control can lead to legal disputes, operational delays, and financial losses from litigation, lease renegotiation, or cancellation.






Warning



Case Study: The Access Road in Fallbrook
We once worked on a storage project in Fallbrook, California. The property sat away from the main road and was not visible from the frontage road. We believed all necessary rights had been secured — until inspectors at the fire department raised concerns about the site’s distance from the main road. After inspection, the fire department required a second access point at the back of the project, requiring new agreements with landowners that the developer had not anticipated. The added expense covered design and engineering of a second access route. Even a route that looks drivable from point A to point B may not be insurable due to fire-code or other regulatory requirements that only surface during inspection.

title: Chapter 2: Verifying Land Control – The Foundation of Acquisition
text:
Land Control & Ownership Disputes
Landowner disputes account for roughly 40% of potential issues encountered in land verification. Title ownership can be held in trust, through corporations, or passed down through inheritance — an heir who says “I control everything” may not actually be on title. Understanding who has true authority over the property is critical before any agreement is signed.






Tip



Case Study: Clearing a Legacy Road Reservation to Ensure Smooth Closing Submitted by Senior Title Insurance Expert Tara Brown-Selders
A developer was advancing a battery storage project in Virginia when title review surfaced a historical municipal roadway reservation. Although the road had never been built and the area had not developed as originally envisioned, the reservation remained in the title record — and the proposed alignment would have cut directly through the planned storage site.
Risk: Even though never built, the municipality technically retained the right to construct the road. The title insurer needed confirmation the municipality no longer intended to pursue it before coverage could be finalized.
Strategy: Rather than waiting for a compressed closing timeline, the developer, legal counsel, title team, and closing team worked together early. A knowledgeable title insurance sales representative — who understood both the developer’s priorities and underwriting requirements — kept the issue visible and helped clarify exactly what language the municipality would need to provide.
Outcome: The municipality provided a confirmation letter stating it had no intent to construct the roadway. Because the issue was flagged months in advance, the letter was secured several weeks before closing, and the transaction proceeded without delay.
Key Takeaway: Early diligence and proactive communication can prevent historical land issues from becoming closing obstacles — and an experienced title professional who understands both the development timeline and underwriting requirements can keep complex issues moving toward resolution.

Power of Attorney
Power of attorney is often statutory in nature, requiring strict adherence to compliance regulations and specific signing protocols. Risks related to unconfirmed authority can produce invalid or unenforceable leases, delays, added costs, ownership disputes, and litigation. Provide the title company with the power of attorney, trust certificate, or corporate records needed to verify signing authority. Small details matter — a different middle initial (George E. Smith vs. George R. Smith) may indicate two different people, and suffixes like Jr. and Sr. must be confirmed to ensure the right parties are under contract.

title: Chapter 2: Verifying Land Control – The Foundation of Acquisition
text:
Joint Tenancy, Trusts & Unrecorded Rights
Developers can be caught off guard by joint tenancy and trusts, and unrecorded rights can be a significant problem even when a title search appears thorough. Landowners often know things the record doesn’t show: capped wells, historical mineral production, an adjacent owner’s access arrangement, or conservation reserve easements that affect how and where you can develop. An apparent access route may not constitute an insurable right — title insurers will require that you “perfect” it, which may mean creating curative documents.
Select a title company with expertise in ALTA coverage and renewable energy transactions, and one that can support the transaction size — not all title carriers can write coverage at the scale many renewable deals require. Establish those relationships early and be clear about your project requirements.

Farmlands & Unrecorded Rights
Grazing and farming leases and water rights are often off-record but represent real third-party interests that need to be addressed. Some jurisdictions, including Illinois, specify deadlines by which notice must be given to farming tenants — miss the notification date and a construction start date tied to it may need to shift.


The Wetlands Challenge
Developing on or near wetlands requires balancing energy needs against the imperative to preserve biodiversity, water quality, and flood control functions. Construction can disturb wetland habitats and the plant and animal life they support, and projects are often subject to regulations such as the North American Wetlands Conservation Act. Ground-mounted systems may require specialized piling techniques to minimize disturbance. Wetlands should be considered during site selection — proximity to water can sometimes shorten cabling runs, but the regulatory complexity often outweighs that benefit.

section: ALTA Surveys and Advanced Title Review: Protecting Site Control
text:
ALTA Surveys and Advanced Title Review: Protecting Site Control
Site control is far more than a signed lease or a marked parcel on a map. Sophisticated buyers, lenders, tax equity investors, and title insurers increasingly expect developers to demonstrate that the legal description aligns precisely with physical realities on the ground.
Too often, early-stage projects rely on outdated boundary sketches or limited title work. A fence crossing a property line, an undefined access route, an abandoned irrigation ditch, or an unrecorded utility easement may seem minor, yet each can materially affect layout, financing certainty, insurability, and the ability to close.
An ALTA/NSPS Land Title Survey identifies visible encroachments, access routes, rights-of-way, improvements, utility corridors, and easements affecting the property, and establishes accurate monumentation. Interconnection corridors, collector lines, substations, battery storage locations, turbine setbacks, and access roads all rely on accurate legal descriptions — inconsistencies discovered after financing documents are drafted can trigger expensive curative work, redesign costs, delayed closings, or threats to tax-credit qualification timelines.
Not all ALTA surveys provide the same protection. Many lenders and institutional investors now require full Tier-1 ALTA surveys with extended coverage and lender-specific certifications. Limited survey products that reduce upfront cost frequently shift risk downstream into financing and closing, where remediation is more expensive and time-sensitive.
A survey alone cannot identify all project risks — advanced title review must examine historical conveyances, easements, restrictions, mortgages, rights-of-way, and prior reservations. Some of the most significant risks (neighbor access arrangements, oral farming leases, historical roadway reservations, irrigation rights, unrecorded utility agreements, conservation restrictions, legacy covenants) are not immediately visible in public records. Experienced teams work with title counsel, surveyors, and underwriters to clarify exceptions and obtain accurate exhibits — through boundary line agreements, easement relocations, subordination agreements, corrective deeds, or escrow arrangements.

title: Chapter 3: Ensuring Correct Ownership – Getting the Signatures Right
text:
Five Common Mistakes
Before a renewable energy project can be built, developers must secure legal rights to use the land — leases, purchase options, and access agreements. Delays or gaps in site control can stall the project and alarm investors. Securing valid agreements hinges on obtaining signatures from all rightful owners of the land. Overlooking ownership complexities can render leases unenforceable and introduce significant risk: Have the right people signed? Have you reviewed deeds? Has a title search been completed?

title: Chapter 3: Ensuring Correct Ownership – Getting the Signatures Right
text:
Five Common Signature Mistakes
  
    
    1. Assuming legal access exists without a deeded easement
    
    2. Not verifying ownership across the entire site
    
    3. Skipping the title commitment review
    
    4. Letting land agreements sit without updates
    
    5. Assuming curative work can wait
  


1. Assuming Legal Access Exists
A road shown on a map does not guarantee legal access. Easements may be missing, expired, or simply unrecorded. Check for a deeded easement — if the project relies on verbal agreements, historical arrangements, or goodwill, it is at risk. Confirm legal access for all parcels and record necessary easements.


2. Not Verifying Ownership Across the Entire Site
Multiple individuals can share ownership, particularly with large or inherited family lands. Records may not reflect recent changes — deaths, trusts, quitclaims. If even one owner is missing from a signature block, the lease or option might not be valid. Initiate curative work to identify and resolve ownership discrepancies, outdated instruments, and missing interests; engaging land specialists can expedite this process.


3. Skipping the Title Commitment Review
The title commitment is where red flags hide: mineral rights carve-outs, old mortgages, utility easements, or overlapping rights from past deals. These are frequently overlooked deal breakers. Order and review title commitments, identifying exceptions related to mineral leases, water rights, environmental restrictions, or cultural heritage sites.


4. Letting Land Agreements Sit Without Updates
A letter of intent or option signed years ago may now be expired, incorrect, or missing parcels that need renegotiation. Align ALTA survey boundaries with title and landowner agreements, cross-reference leases and maps with legal descriptions, and ensure all site control documents are valid, assignable, and fully executed.


5. Assuming Curative Work Can Wait
Curative work takes time. Probate, corporate consents, and lien releases can take months — wait too long to fix gaps in ownership, access, or title, and it’s often too late. Start early; everything takes longer than you think.






Note



Curative Is a Relay Race
Title curative is rarely a one-time exercise. It requires ongoing coordination among land teams, surveyors, legal counsel, title underwriters, lenders, and developers. Successful projects establish clear communication channels, assign ownership responsibility early, and maintain structured follow-up to ensure defects are resolved before financing deadlines. Title curative is often the linchpin of a successful financing close — systematically identifying defects, prioritizing cures, coordinating stakeholders, and managing residual exposure through escrows and endorsements can materially reduce delays and improve financing certainty.

Common Ownership Complexities

Life Estates: Grant an individual rights to a property for their lifetime (e.g., deeded to Mr. and Mrs. Smith with a reservation that Grandma retains a life estate). If Grandma hasn’t signed, the agreement is incomplete and not insurable.
Joint Tenancy and Tenancy in Common: Properties owned by multiple individuals with equal or proportionate shares — all owners must consent and sign for the agreement to be valid.
Trusts and Corporate Entities: Require signatures from authorized representatives; verification of authority is essential.
Unrecorded Interests: Rights or claims not reflected in public records, such as verbal agreements or unrecorded easements.

In one instance, a developer failed to recognize that a life estate holder had not signed the lease. The oversight surfaced during financing, and the project faced significant delays while the developer renegotiated with the life estate holder, who then demanded more favorable terms.

Case Study: Racing Probate
During a recent closing, signed lease amendments were needed from all landowners involved. Learning that one woman’s health was failing, the team prioritized her signature so the amendment could be recorded quickly. To sign for the trust, the daughter needs a physician’s letter (HIPAA-compliant, consistent with the trust’s terms) confirming the mother’s incapacity. title: Chapter 4: Unseen Challenges – Navigating Mineral Rights
text:
Tribal Mineral Rights Complexity
You can’t control the sun or the wind, but you can control your mineral risk.
When acquiring land, it is important to understand that there are surface rights and there are severed rights — rights separate from surface ownership. Mineral rights refer to ownership of underground minerals; a subsurface severance refers to minerals legally separated from the surface estate. Because mineral rights laws vary significantly by jurisdiction, developers should consult qualified legal counsel and title professionals regarding project-specific risks and compliance obligations.
In many states, mineral rights can be separated from surface rights, allowing different owners for underground resources and the land above. The mineral owner typically holds the dominant estate — the right to access the surface to extract minerals.
On tribal lands, the federal government may own the subsurface estate while private individuals or tribes own the surface — often set for a fixed term (a term mineral interest), after which rights return to the surface owner. This is most common in Texas and other states with complex oil and gas law. Mineral rights on tribal lands may involve separate federal oversight or distinct tribal governance requirements; surface and subsurface rights are not always aligned, and additional approvals may be required before development can proceed. Developers should approach tribal projects as long-term government-to-government relationships rather than conventional land acquisitions — success depends as much on trust, transparency, and cultural understanding as on contractual structure.

When minerals are severed from the surface estate, the property has two chains of title: one for the surface, one for the subsurface. While the surface chain can usually be reviewed by a title company, the subsurface requires a specialized search known as a Mineral Ownership Report (MOR).
Unlike a standard title commitment, an MOR often traces ownership back to the 1800s.

Heirs may inherit rights they don’t know exist; leases are forgotten; rights go unexercised until energy prices make them valuable. Developers can encounter “breaks” in the chain where ownership is unclear or fragmented across generations. For M&A due diligence, the implications are profound:

Time — these searches can take months, making early detection critical.
Cost — curative work to resolve gaps, probate issues, or missing heirs can run high.
Insurability — subsurface rights must be affirmatively insured just like surface rights, or deals risk collapse at closing.







Important



Key M&A Takeaway: If a potential severance is flagged, order MORs immediately. Ignoring subsurface rights until late in the deal often results in closing delays, renegotiations, or failed transactions.

Implications for Renewable Energy Projects

Surface Disruption: Mineral rights holders are typically entitled to access and use the surface for extraction.
Operational Risks: Drilling or mining may disrupt renewable facility operations — and this risk does not disappear simply because production is inactive at acquisition. Existing mineral owners may retain rights to future access, pipelines, or production infrastructure that could interfere with operations years or decades later.
Insurance Limitations: Title insurance policies may exclude mineral rights issues, increasing risk.

The government reserves mineral rights on land grant deeds west of the Mississippi, often superseding private ownership — developers should examine deed specifics and government reservations carefully. While the U.S. government rarely exercises its right to extract minerals from private land, mineral resources (oil, gas, coal) carry distinct legal rights and risks, and shallow versus deep well rights can vary significantly by depth.

text:
Why Mineral Rights Matter: Severance and Two Chains of Title
Severance occurs when subsurface rights are legally separated from surface rights. Types of mineral severance include royalty interests (NPRI & ORRI), leasehold/working interests, split estates, term severances, and fee simple severances.
Without severance, there is one chain of title and one title commitment. With severance, developers face two separate chains of title, multiple ownership interests, additional title review requirements, and separate risk mitigation obligations — which can create title insurance gaps, financing delays, access conflicts, and increased legal and curative costs.

    Surface Estate
    Standard title search · county records · single ownership history
    Reviewed by conventional title company

    
    Subsurface (Mineral) Estate
    Separate chain of title · may trace back 150+ years
    Requires Mineral Ownership Report (MOR)

title: Chapter 4: Unseen Challenges – Navigating Mineral Rights
text:
Dormant vs. Producing Mineral Rights

  Dormant vs. Producing Mineral Rights
  
    
    Dormant
    No production history
    Records often incomplete
    Heirs hard to locate
    Risk = uncertainty
    Needs reconstruction
    
    Producing
    Active leases / operators
    Easier to trace ownership
    Mineral estate often dominant
    Risk = operational conflict
    Needs negotiation
  

One of the most important questions developers should ask in early diligence: “Has there ever been production on this property, or even an attempt to produce?”
Dormant mineral rights may appear harmless because no active drilling is taking place — but dormant does not mean extinguished. Ownership records may be incomplete, heirs may be impossible to locate easily, and interests may be divided among many descendants. Reconstructing those chains can require probate review, heirship verification, and historical title analysis stretching back generations. The risk here is uncertainty — not knowing who owns the rights or whether claims may surface later.
Producing mineral rights create a different exposure. Ownership is often easier to trace because operators have already researched the estate, but active production introduces operational conflicts: in many jurisdictions the mineral estate is dominant over the surface estate, so operators may retain broad rights to access and use the surface for extraction — directly affecting solar arrays, turbine placement, battery storage, access roads, and collector systems. Historical production from abandoned or capped wells may carry lingering legal issues if leases were never formally terminated; active production typically requires negotiated surface use waivers, subordination agreements, or non-disturbance arrangements; exploration leases mean operators retain the right to initiate future activity.
Comprehensive due diligence should review production history, lease activity, operator records, and oil and gas databases, and determine whether surface use agreements exist or permit filings suggest future development interest. These findings directly influence valuation, underwriting, financing terms, and construction planning. Title insurers evaluate active and historical mineral activity more closely than dormant estates, and underwriters may require recorded surface use waivers or subordinations — or exclude mineral-related risk from coverage entirely if adequate protection can’t be secured.






Note



Timing is critical. Mineral ownership research, negotiations with operators, and curative work can take months. Projects that identify these risks early retain far greater flexibility to redesign layouts, negotiate agreements, adjust valuation assumptions, or sequence financing. Proactively approached operators can become valuable partners in resolving mineral risk rather than obstacles to development.

title: Chapter 4: Unseen Challenges – Navigating Mineral Rights
section: Mineral Rights Are a Bankability Trigger
text:
Mineral Rights Are a Bankability Trigger
Mineral rights are not simply a title issue — they are a bankability issue. Lenders, tax equity investors, and future acquirers increasingly require developers to identify and mitigate mineral risks before financing can proceed. Standard title insurance often excludes mineral-related risk unless specialized endorsements, curative actions, or a separate mineral ownership analysis are obtained. Even balance-sheet-financed projects may face future transaction challenges if mineral exposure remains unresolved.






Tip



Case Study: Rethinking Mineral Surface Waiver Requirements Submitted by Senior Title Insurance Expert Tara Brown-Selders
A battery energy storage system (BESS) project in Texas presented an opportunity to evaluate mineral risk differently than traditional solar development. For solar projects, developers typically obtain surface waivers from 100% of mineral owners to prevent drilling from interfering with arrays and infrastructure. This battery storage site consisted of roughly thirty acres, but the equipment itself would occupy only ten acres.
Risk: The standard approach would have required surface waivers from every mineral interest holder across the entire property — costly and time-consuming for a project using only a third of the land.
Strategy: The developer, relying on a trusted title insurance sales representative, proposed obtaining waivers only across the portion of the property where the battery storage equipment would actually sit. Multiple conversations reviewed the site plan and the acreage that would remain available if mineral development ever occurred. The team evaluated the issue through a project-specific lens rather than defaulting to standard practice.
Outcome: Underwriting agreed that surface waivers needed to cover only about 30% of the property rather than the full acreage. The project moved forward with appropriate title coverage while preserving operational flexibility across the rest of the land — avoiding unnecessary time and expense.
Key Takeaway: New project types and land-use patterns call for project-specific mineral risk analysis rather than blanket application of solar-industry norms. An experienced title professional who understands both development and underwriting perspectives can bridge the two and unlock practical solutions.

text:
Data Room Readiness
In the fast-paced world of mergers and acquisitions, companies often face tight deadlines to complete critical due diligence. It’s important to be thorough but efficient so that no key issue is overlooked. M&A transactions typically allow 60 to 90 days for due diligence — often only 60, so teams must quickly understand what needs to be done.
In accelerated transaction environments, projects with organized documentation, clear site control, completed diligence, and well-structured data rooms command greater market interest and move through financing more efficiently than less-prepared assets. Pipeline prioritization is critical.
Well-organized data rooms containing current title materials, surveys, permits, leases, environmental reports, and financing documentation significantly accelerate acquisition review and improve buyer confidence during compressed timelines. An energy company successfully completed due diligence within a 60-day window by prioritizing critical leases and deploying a specialized team on high-risk areas, avoiding delays that would otherwise have surfaced later.

text:
Front-Loaded Diligence
Unresolved mineral issues discovered late in financing can jeopardize closing timelines, increase curative costs, and create lender concern. Successful projects rely on front-loaded diligence and proactive negotiation long before financing milestones are reached. Experienced ALTA surveyors play an important role at closing — coordinating with title teams, responding to underwriting comments, revising certifications, and resolving boundary or access issues that arise during final review. Local and regional experience matters: surveyors and title professionals familiar with county-level practices and jurisdiction-specific requirements often resolve issues more efficiently than firms without that history.

title: Chapter 5: Racing the Clock – Due Diligence Strategies for Tight Timelines
text:
Government Agency Timing Risk
Compressed timelines create unique challenges when projects involve state or local government land. Public-sector approvals require multiple layers of internal review, legal oversight, and administrative coordination that rarely align with commercial financing schedules. Even straightforward agreements — access easements, road crossings, school trust lands, water districts, county-owned parcels — may require review by agency counsel, governing boards, procurement departments, or state attorneys general before approval, and these reviews are rarely accelerated for financing deadlines.
Public agencies are often balancing competing priorities with limited personnel and aging administrative systems, so seemingly minor revisions to legal descriptions or formatting can create unexpected delays late in the process. Checkerboard ownership compounds this: developers may complete diligence on privately controlled land only to discover a single state-owned access corridor or utility crossing remains unresolved — and because these often involve critical infrastructure, unresolved approvals can quickly become financing blockers.
Developers should identify all government-controlled parcels early and prioritize approvals for access roads, substations, collector systems, and transmission corridors as critical path items, not secondary administrative tasks. Relationship management — open communication with agency staff, surveyors, and legal reviewers — is often as valuable as understanding the legal requirements themselves.

Real World Considerations
Exclusivity agreements are commonly signed during fast-paced negotiations, and the acquiring party must identify all issues within the set timeframe. The first recommended step: understand the intent of the transaction. Is it market share? A technology bet? Cash flow? The reason for acquiring guides everything that follows.
Prioritize key parcels to manage tight timeframes — start by identifying project improvements and locating medium voltage, high voltage, interconnection, substation, and access points. High-risk issues vary by client and by project stage; M&A deals can happen early (where it’s mostly a matter of site control) or at later, shovel-ready stages, and the risk profile shifts accordingly.

Many developers use consolidated title review, or “Red Light” reports, to centralize title exceptions, survey encroachments, lease expirations, and unresolved curative items into a single tracking framework, helping teams prioritize and coordinate cure strategies across legal, survey, title, and development.

Assemble a multidisciplinary team, varying composition by project, ensure everyone understands their responsibilities, critical deadlines, and the focus of the work, and maintain regular communication with stakeholders.






Warning



Verifying Information Is Critical
A seller, asked about a permitting issue, said: “Don’t worry, it’s all taken care of. Not a problem.” When construction was about to begin, the team discovered the permitting issue had never been resolved — causing unexpected delays and significant cost. Get all information and documentation from the prospective seller, then conduct your own independent due diligence. Don’t take representations at face value.

Strategies for Due Diligence Under Time Constraints
Prioritize Key Areas: Focus on land essential for project infrastructure and areas with potential legal or environmental complications.
Examine Existing Documentation: Review all seller-provided materials comprehensively and flag missing or incomplete information for follow-up.
Identify Stakeholders: Landowners, residents, community groups, and government agencies. Focus initial efforts on landowners whose property is central to feasibility and construction footprint.
Engage with Landowners: Establish transparent, consistent communication; ask about unrecorded agreements, mineral rights, and environmental concerns; build trust and give landowners a sense of involvement.






Note



Timing and Narrative Control: The earliest public narrative surrounding a project can significantly influence community perception and permitting outcomes. Delayed or reactive engagement allows opposition groups to frame the project negatively before developers establish trust. If you don’t control the messaging for your project, others will — and on social media, that can become a disaster. Know what’s been posted, verify whether it’s truthful, and address opposition directly rather than letting it surface for the first time in a hearing.


Assemble a Multidisciplinary Team Including an ALTA Surveyor. title: Chapter 6: Environmental and Site Considerations in Project Acquisitions
text:
Environmental Site Assessment (ESA)
Environmental factors are critical in determining a project’s feasibility, impacting site suitability, regulatory compliance, community acceptance, and long-term viability.
An ESA identifies potential environmental impacts through site inspections, historical records review, government agency research, and analysis of biodiversity, land use, water resources, soil conditions, and local socio-economic impacts. It establishes the presence of hazardous materials and evaluates risks to human health and the environment, including water safety and air quality. An expert assessment ensures negative impacts are identified, minimized, or avoided before development proceeds.
Key components include: government agency records research; physical and ecological characteristics; biological environment; water resources; air quality; human health; cultural heritage; community impact; hazardous materials and contamination; risk assessment; and an Environmental Management Plan (EMP) that governs mitigation through decommissioning.

title: Chapter 6: Environmental and Site Considerations in Project Acquisitions
section: Key Factors That Can Derail a Project
text:
Key Factors That Can Derail a Project

Flood Plains
Flooding can cause catastrophic damage to solar panels, inverters, and other electrical equipment. Developing in floodplains requires flood risk assessment covering site selection, flood-resilient design, and regulatory compliance — elevated structures, flood-proof electrical components, and attention to the natural flood mitigation services floodplains provide. Floods can occur almost anywhere, not only near water bodies; heavy rains, poor drainage, and nearby construction can create risk. Always check FEMA flood maps, and secure flood insurance once risk is understood.


Protected Species and Habitats
Determine early whether protected species or habitats are present. Request biological assessments and confirm whether wildlife agencies have been contacted and have offered recommendations for legal compliance.






Warning



Case Study: Migratory Birds
A wind energy project we worked on was delayed when it was discovered that the site sat on a migratory pathway for endangered birds. The developer had to implement significant mitigation measures — including curtailment strategies and habitat conservation plans — increasing costs and affecting timelines. Environmental due diligence and community engagement are not just about compliance; they protect the long-term viability and acceptance of the project.
Community engagement recommendations contributed by Ayelet Hines & Mike Casey, Tigercomm.




Wetlands and Water Bodies
Wetlands supply habitat, replenish groundwater, limit flooding, purify drinking water, and enable cultural and recreational activities. Projects affecting wetlands may need Clean Water Act permits — identify wetlands using National Wetlands Inventory (NWI) maps, established by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to provide biologists, planners, and others with data on wetland distribution and type.


Soil and Geotechnical Conditions
Soil and geotechnical reports provide subsurface data needed for safe, stable foundation design — using boreholes, CPT, and laboratory testing to determine soil characteristics, inform foundation selection, and guarantee long-term stability. These reports identify hazards such as slope instability or ground settlement that could affect turbines, arrays, or transmission structures.


Cultural and Historical Sites
Projects can impact historical sites, indigenous lands, and culturally significant landscapes, potentially disturbing archaeological sites containing artifacts, human remains, or historic structures. This often requires archaeological surveys, community consultation, and impact assessments. Development on tribal lands requires compliance with federal, tribal, and state law, and usually needs tribal or landowner approval — the EPA issues environmental permits for sources on tribal lands, and the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) handles leases and right-of-way grants. Tribes can develop their own permitting programs subject to specific qualifying criteria.






Tip



Case Study: Sacred Sites in Wyoming
We once worked on a project in Wyoming where our own site review revealed what looked like piles of rocks. Engaging local stakeholders revealed these were protected historical and cultural tribal artifacts. We negotiated with tribal leaders and local landowners to create easements permitting tribes access to the sacred site for vision quests — easements covering both the property and the project had to be designed for all stakeholders. Understanding those rights, and addressing them early, was essential to keeping the project moving.


The visual character of a landscape can also be culturally significant — large-scale wind turbines or extensive solar arrays can dramatically alter the aesthetic and historic qualities of a region, often leading to community opposition.


Health Protection Zones
In California, “Health Protection Zones” (HPZs) are 3,200-foot buffer zones established by counties around sensitive receptors (homes, schools, hospitals) to protect communities from industrial hazards, measured from the property line or building footprint depending on setback distance. Rather than dictating general building practices, these zones strictly regulate the proximity and operations of the oil and gas industry. Other jurisdictions, including parts of Illinois, maintain their own health protection zones near cities. If you’re purchasing a 200 MW project — or a 1,000 MW portfolio — you don’t want to discover significant land use issues after acquisition. Get to know community leaders and influencers; they can flag potential issues long before formal review.

text:
Community Acceptance
Community acceptance has moved up the ladder of importance in transactions. Resistance stems from environmental impact concerns, economic fears, and aesthetic objections, compounded by a lack of early engagement, insufficient information, and distrust of developers or project governance. Overcoming resistance requires early dialogue, clear communication of project benefits and local gains, addressing specific concerns directly, and establishing long-term trust through local empowerment and developer commitment.
Community engagement should be treated as a core component of project risk management, not a secondary public relations function. Early engagement, consistent communication, and proactive outreach can materially reduce permitting delays, litigation risk, and transaction uncertainty.

text:
Navigating Tribal Lands and Sovereign Jurisdictions
Renewable energy development on tribal lands involves unique legal, regulatory, and governance considerations because federally recognized tribes operate as sovereign nations. Tribal lands are frequently held in trust by the federal government, and development may require approvals and enforceability considerations that differ substantially from conventional private-land transactions. Tribal governance structures, leadership transitions, and community priorities may evolve during development, making trust, transparency, and consistent engagement essential to successful execution.

Build these additional approval timelines into project schedules, financing assumptions, and transaction risk assessments.

section: Opposition Risk Is a Material Development Risk
text:
Opposition Risk Is a Material Development Risk
Organized opposition groups have successfully delayed or blocked utility-scale renewable projects through political campaigns, public hearings, litigation threats, and social media activism — materially affecting permitting certainty, development timelines, financing schedules, and project valuation. Developers should be prepared to address misinformation and rapidly evolving public narratives; social media and organized opposition can accelerate resistance if engagement is delayed or inconsistent.
Local communities are rarely homogeneous: landowners benefiting from lease revenue, local businesses expecting economic activity, government entities anticipating tax revenue, and residents who perceive little direct benefit will all respond differently. Effective engagement strategies should be tailored to each group’s interests, concerns, and motivations.

Key Takeaways

An Environmental Site Assessment is not a formality — it is the basis for permitting, financing, and long-term operational compliance, including decommissioning planning.
Tribal land, cultural heritage, and BIA approval risk demand a government-to-government relationship mindset rather than a conventional transactional approach.
Community opposition is a material, quantifiable transaction risk, not a soft public relations issue — and it should be priced into valuation and timeline assumptions.
Local zoning innovations like California’s Health Protection Zones can override or delay development even where mineral or land rights are otherwise clear.
Controlling the narrative early, and treating community stakeholders as differentiated groups rather than a monolith, materially reduces permitting and litigation risk.

title: Chapter 7: Hidden Layers – Addressing Complex Ownership Structures in Project Acquisitions
text:
Hidden Ownership Complexities
M&A has become one of the fastest ways to fill pipeline gaps in the renewable sector. With interconnection queues stretching for years and greenfield development slowing under regulatory and community pressure, acquiring projects can be the most effective path forward. But there’s a catch: deals that look strong on paper can fall apart at closing. The reason is almost always the same — risk buried in the details, such as land ownership issues or missing signatures that weren’t uncovered early enough.
Every deal carries risk. The question is whether you identify those risks early, when they can be managed, or later, when they threaten valuation and delay closing.
Ownership isn’t always straightforward. Overlooking a single signatory can render a lease unenforceable; unrecorded rights, which often exist, can completely derail financing. Common issues include:
It is critical to look beyond the deed — confirm signatory authority and identify unrecorded interests through landowner conversations. Don’t assume the title report tells the whole story.

title: Chapter 7: Hidden Layers – Addressing Complex Ownership Structures in Project Acquisitions
text:
Life Estates: If the life tenant hasn’t signed, the agreement is incomplete.
Trusts & Estates: Require specific authorization to bind the entity.
Easements and Rights-of-Way: Allow third parties to use parts of the property, potentially limiting development or requiring adjustments.
Undivided Interests: All co-owners must consent to lease terms.
Encumbrances and Liens: Claims by creditors or other parties that need to be resolved or subordinated.
Probate Complications: Missing heirs can stall transactions for years.
Off-Record Agreements: Grazing leases, water rights, or off-record access can create conflicts.

title: Chapter 7: Hidden Layers – Addressing Complex Ownership Structures in Project Acquisitions
text:
Life Estates

  
  Life Estate: Two Interests, One Property
  
    
    Life Tenant
    Possesses & uses property
    for their lifetime
    
    Remainderman
    Receives full ownership
    upon tenant's death
  
  
  at death

A life estate is a legal ownership interest lasting for the duration of the “life tenant’s” life, dividing ownership into two interests: the right to possess and use the property during the tenant’s lifetime, and the right to receive the property after death (the “remainderman”). The life tenant cannot leave the property to heirs — their interest ends automatically at death. For example, a deed reading “To John Doe for life, then to Jane Doe” gives John a life estate; upon his death, Jane automatically receives full ownership. The life tenant’s consent is required for any lease or agreement affecting their interest, so their signature must be on all related agreements.
crumbs: 14  Chapter 7: Hidden Layers – Addressing Complex Ownership Structures in Project Acquisitions

title: Chapter 7: Hidden Layers – Addressing Complex Ownership Structures in Project Acquisitions
text:
Trusts & Estates

  
  Trust Structure: Three Stakeholders
  
    Grantor
    Trustmanaged by Trustee
    Beneficiary
  
  
    
  
  Trustee must verify authority & terms before signing any agreement

A trust is a legal arrangement to manage and distribute assets, moving ownership from the original owner to the trust. Three stakeholders are typically involved: the grantor (who places assets into the trust), the trustee (who manages the assets for the beneficiaries’ benefit), and the beneficiary (who receives the assets once trust conditions are met). Trusts may be revocable (changeable by the grantor while alive) or irrevocable (difficult or impossible to change once established). Establishing a trust allows the grantor and beneficiaries to avoid probate, which can cause major delays because all heirs must sign documents related to transactions. Trust property requires trustee action and verification of both their authority and the trust’s terms.

title: Chapter 7: Hidden Layers – Addressing Complex Ownership Structures in Project Acquisitions
text:
Easements and Rights-of-Way
An easement is a legal right for a non-owner to use another’s land for a specific purpose; a right-of-way is a specific type of easement granting the right to travel or pass across property. All rights-of-way are easements, but not all easements are rights-of-way — easements can also cover utility lines or support for structures.






Note



Illinois Example: Easements in Practice
In Illinois, renewable energy projects rely on private land easements and public right-of-way agreements, with landowners typically negotiating voluntary lease and easement agreements guided by the state’s Department of Agriculture and setback rules protecting agricultural land and drainage.

Agricultural Impact Mitigation Agreements (AIMAs): Developers of large-scale wind and solar farms must negotiate an AIMA with the Illinois Department of Agriculture before construction, ensuring farmland is restored to pre-construction condition and crop losses are compensated.
Easement Types: Access easements for roads, utility easements for transmission lines, and “solar/wind rights” easements that prohibit adjacent owners from building structures or planting trees that block sunlight or wind.
Right-of-Way: Developers frequently need to cross or tie into public road rights-of-way; under model ordinances, wind turbines are typically set back at least 1.1 times their maximum blade tip height from the center point of public road rights-of-way.
State Setback & Drainage Protections: Recent legislation limits local control to reasonable regulations — municipalities cannot outright ban renewable development — and facility owners are authorized to cross drainage systems during construction, provided they restore the land as soon as practicable.

Illinois is just one example. Always check each state and county for its own easement and right-of-way requirements.
crumbs: 14  Chapter 7: Hidden Layers – Addressing Complex Ownership Structures in Project Acquisitions

title: Chapter 7: Hidden Layers – Addressing Complex Ownership Structures in Project Acquisitions
text:
Undivided Interests
An undivided interest is a form of shared ownership where multiple parties hold rights to an entire property rather than a specific portion — each co-owner possesses an equal right to the whole, defined by a percentage share. For instance, three siblings who inherit a property each hold a one-third undivided interest in the entire residence, and all co-owners must agree to lease or sale terms.
crumbs: 14  Chapter 7: Hidden Layers – Addressing Complex Ownership Structures in Project Acquisitions

title: Chapter 7: Hidden Layers – Addressing Complex Ownership Structures in Project Acquisitions
text:
Encumbrances and Liens
An encumbrance is a claim on a property limiting the owner’s ability to use it; a lien is a specific type of encumbrance representing a financial claim securing repayment of debt. Encumbrances can also be non-financial — an easement allowing someone else to use part of the property, or a deed restriction limiting development. Claims by creditors or other parties may need to be resolved or subordinated before closing.
crumbs: 14  Chapter 7: Hidden Layers – Addressing Complex Ownership Structures in Project Acquisitions

title: Chapter 7: Hidden Layers – Addressing Complex Ownership Structures in Project Acquisitions
text:
Probate Complications
Missing or unlocatable heirs are a significant complication in probate — the executor must locate and inform all beneficiaries before assets can be distributed, leading to delays that can stall transactions for years and require extensive skip tracing (finding hard-to-locate beneficiaries or witnesses). This can be especially complex for large estates with extensive family trees or estranged or geographically dispersed members. The court has a legal obligation to ensure all beneficiaries are notified, creating a mandatory pause until all heirs are found or a reasonable effort to locate them has been exhausted. Probate complications affect mineral rights searches as well.

    2. Life Estates, Trusts & Entities — who actually has authority to sign
    
    3. Easements, Rights-of-Way & Undivided Interests — competing claims to the same land
    
    4. Liens & Encumbrances — creditor and third-party claims requiring resolution
    
    5. Off-Record & Probate Risk — what the title report can't show at all

Off-Record Agreements
Unrecorded agreements related to property use — grazing leases, water rights, off-record access — may be legally binding between the original parties, yet lack public notice. This creates issues for buyers or lenders unaware of the rights or restrictions, potentially leading to conflicting ownership claims or title defects.

Strategies for Unveiling and Addressing Complexities
Title Examination: Review the chain of title and all recorded documents; identify all parties with a legal interest. Engage real estate attorneys experienced in complex ownership issues.
Owner Communication: Directly contact owners to understand unrecorded interests or agreements; use questionnaires to gather detailed information.

Negotiation and Resolution: Proactively address disputes or claims and negotiate terms acceptable to all parties.

Real-World Example
A solar project was halted when a previously unknown easement allowed a utility company to install transmission lines across the property, conflicting with the project’s layout. The developer had to renegotiate with the utility, causing delays and additional costs.

title: Chapter 8: Enhancing Collaboration Between M&A and Development Teams
text:
Team Alignment Is a Deal Accelerator
Successful project acquisition and development hinge on effective collaboration between commercial (M&A) teams and development teams. The consequences of misalignment include inefficiencies, project delays, cost overruns, and strained workplace relationships. Successful transaction teams establish clear ownership responsibilities, regular status reviews, and structured follow-up procedures to prevent unresolved defects from delaying financing or closing.
Alignment between commercial, development, legal, title, permitting, and financing teams can materially influence transaction outcomes. Misaligned assumptions about timelines, site control, permitting complexity, or construction sequencing often lead to valuation gaps, financing delays, cost overruns, and reduced returns.
Renewable energy closings often depend on centralized transaction management. Unified closing protocols that coordinate legal documentation, title review, surveys, escrow instructions, lender requirements, and execution timelines can significantly reduce closing delays and improve financing certainty. Strategic communications, stakeholder engagement, and political awareness should also be integrated into broader project execution and risk management strategies.

Integrated Expert Teams

Siloed diligence creates conflicting assumptions, delayed issue identification, and avoidable transaction risk. Many developers establish preferred relationships with surveyors, title professionals, environmental consultants, and legal teams familiar with renewable transactions — repeat collaboration improves communication, accelerates issue resolution, and creates greater consistency across projects and portfolios. Integrated milestone calendars align permitting deadlines, title curative milestones, EPC schedules, PPA obligations, financing timelines, and COD targets into a centralized tracking framework shared across commercial and development teams.

title: Chapter 9: Accurately Assessing Worth and Timing in Renewable Energy M&A
text:
Why COD Matters for Acquisitions
Accurate valuation is a fundamental component of successful M&A transactions. The Commercial Operation Date (COD) is critical in evaluating renewable project acquisitions because it signifies the point at which the project is fully operational, grid-connected, and ready to produce energy under its Power Purchase Agreement (PPA). COD triggers major financial events: release of final project funding, the off-taker’s obligation to purchase power at the contracted rate, and the transition from construction to operational security. An earlier COD can increase valuation by accelerating revenue and decreasing project risk.
Revenue Generation Trigger: COD marks the start of revenue-generating activity, as the off-taker becomes contractually obligated to purchase power under the PPA.
Financing Milestones: COD often aligns with the release of remaining project funding and tax equity investment. Delays in survey completion, unresolved title matters, or unmet ALTA endorsement requirements can directly impact financing timelines, construction loan closings, and tax equity transactions — coordinate survey, title, underwriting, and financing teams early to avoid last-minute closing disruptions.
Performance Guarantees: COD sets the baseline for post-operation performance guarantees, including energy output, which can trigger penalties if not met.
PPA Security Transition: The PPA’s financial security requirements shift from construction-period security to post-commercial-operation security at COD, affecting the asset’s financial profile and valuation.

Even minor title defects or unresolved survey issues can delay funding or jeopardize ITC/PTC qualification.
Developers and tax-equity investors frequently use title-risk reserves or targeted escrows to manage unresolved defects while preserving financing schedules. Structured release mechanisms tied to curative milestones help align incentives between sponsors, investors, title underwriters, and lenders while limiting open-ended exposure.

text:
Project De-Risking and Valuation Before/After COD

  Valuation Before vs. After COD

    "Developer fee" transaction

Projects sold before COD are essentially “developer fee” transactions, where value derives from completed development milestones; the price reflects development work and future revenue potential. Projects at or near COD are significantly de-risked and valued on proven cash flow and operational performance, making them more attractive to investors.






Note



“Project Slippage” as a Valuation Risk
Buyers and investors increasingly evaluate “project slippage” risk when assessing renewable energy portfolios. Delays involving permitting, title curative, interconnection, mineral rights, or community opposition may materially reduce the likelihood that projects meet financing and construction deadlines — directly affecting valuation and marketability. Minor title defects, survey inconsistencies, or lease discrepancies discovered late in financing can create disproportionate impacts, including lender holdbacks, delayed funding, increased curative costs, and threats to ITC/PTC timelines.

A lease lapse prior to financing or commercial operation can create material transaction and valuation risk — overlay lease calendars against COD/PTC timelines and treat unresolved extensions as a flag, not a footnote.

The Impact of Timing on Valuation

COD Targets: Pivotal in determining a project’s value, especially when aligned with market demand or regulatory incentives.
Market Conditions: Energy prices, technology costs, and policy environments fluctuate, affecting project economics.

Developers should periodically conduct strategic pipeline reviews to identify which projects are most likely to achieve COD within required financing or tax-credit timelines. Projects facing significant title, permitting, interconnection, community, or site-control risk may require restructuring, acceleration, or monetization before market conditions change.






Warning



Policy Changes Compress M&A Timelines. Legislative and policy changes can suddenly compress the entire transaction market. Tax credit revisions and evolving “start construction” requirements can rapidly compress development and M&A timelines, increasing pressure to advance projects into construction, accelerate financing, or monetize assets quickly before incentive qualification windows narrow.

text:
Adjusting Valuation Based on Due Diligence

Risk Assessment: Quantify risks identified during diligence (legal, environmental) and adjust the discount rate or required return accordingly.
Underwriting Deficiencies: Unclear policy language creates litigation risk.
Cost Implications: Estimate additional costs to resolve issues (legal fees, remediation) and incorporate them into the financial model.
Timing Delays: Reassess cash flow projections for potential delays and the impact on deadline-tied incentives.

Permitting risk and community opposition should be incorporated into project risk assessments and valuation models — evaluate public sentiment, local political dynamics, prior permitting history, and evidence of organized opposition when assessing timelines and financial exposure.

text:
Cost, Risk & Residual Risk Management
A comprehensive document audit at the outset reveals potential risk factors — every issue can be boiled down to a cost, and once a cost is assigned, a mitigation strategy (insurance or another indemnity instrument) can be developed. Not all title defects require immediate physical resolution before closing; developers and lenders may use escrows, endorsements, indemnities, or structured underwriting solutions to manage residual risk while preserving financing timelines.






Tip



We recently closed a rare case where we had to file a title claim on behalf of a client and were successful in obtaining coverage for the legal costs involved in resolving the issue — the title company ultimately covered the legal resolution costs. Title insurance remains one of the most effective tools for identifying and mitigating risk that survives even the most thorough diligence.


Tribal land transactions may involve additional financing and enforceability considerations — sovereign immunity, federal trust structures, and jurisdictional limitations can affect lender remedies, collateral rights, and dispute resolution. Engage experienced legal counsel and title professionals early when evaluating tribal land projects.






Warning



Case Study Insight
A company acquired a project expecting COD in 2026. Due diligence revealed permitting delays that could push COD to 2028, significantly affecting the project’s net present value. The company renegotiated the purchase price to reflect the new timeline and associated risks.

title: Chapter 10: Inheriting a Project – Navigating the Challenges and Leveraging Opportunities
text:
Fast-Transaction Readiness
M&A is the key to filling pipeline gaps. With increasingly complex market and regulatory conditions, treat every renewable acquisition as if you’re buying development execution capability under extreme time pressure, not just development potential under favorable market conditions. This demands a holistic approach combining meticulous due diligence, strategic collaboration, and proactive risk management.
Acquiring existing projects offers a shortcut to market entry, but also presents unique challenges. At some point, every project will be the subject of a transaction — debt for Notice to Proceed (NTP) and start of construction, tax equity at operations, purchase or sale, whatever it might be. Ensuring everything is ready for financial closing requires thorough due diligence.
Developers anticipating potential divestitures or accelerated sales should prepare projects for rapid diligence review by organizing title materials, surveys, permits, lease portfolios, interconnection documentation, and environmental records in advance. Market-ready projects transact more efficiently under compressed market conditions.

title: Chapter 11: The Fundamentals of Project Finance for Electricity and Renewable Energy
text:
Introduction
By Michael DeLucia, Adjunct Faculty, New York University, Instructor, Project Finance for Electricity and Renewable Energy
The global transition to cleaner energy systems is reshaping the way electricity infrastructure is developed and financed. Large-scale solar farms, wind projects, battery storage facilities, and hybrid energy systems now require billions of dollars in investment each year. Unlike traditional corporate investments funded directly from a company’s balance sheet, most modern energy projects rely on project finance — a specialized financial structure designed to fund large capital-intensive assets while allocating risk among multiple stakeholders.
Project finance for electricity and renewable energy is typically a non-recourse or limited-recourse financing method where funds for projects like wind or solar farms are repaid solely from the project’s generated cash flow rather than the developer’s balance sheet. It uses a special purpose vehicle (SPV) to isolate risk, with debt secured by long-term contracts like Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs). Lenders, investors, utilities, governments, and communities all play roles in shaping the success or failure of an energy project.
This chapter introduces the core principles of project finance as applied to electricity generation, particularly renewable and hybrid systems such as solar-plus-storage or wind integrated with battery assets. It explains how energy projects are structured, how capital is raised, and how developers and investors manage risk throughout the life cycle of a project. Understanding these fundamentals is essential for anyone working in energy development, infrastructure investment, or climate-focused finance.

title: Chapter 11: The Fundamentals of Project Finance for Electricity and Renewable Energy
section: The Evolution of Energy Project Finance
text:
The Evolution of Energy Project Finance
Electricity infrastructure has historically been one of the most capital-intensive sectors of the global economy. Traditional power plants — coal, natural gas, or nuclear facilities — required massive upfront investments and long development timelines.
In earlier decades, these projects were typically financed directly by regulated utilities, which recovered costs through electricity rates paid by consumers. However, energy market liberalization and the growth of independent power producers led to a shift in financing structures.
Project finance emerged as a preferred model because it allows:

Large infrastructure projects to be financed without overburdening corporate balance sheets
Risks to be allocated across multiple participants
Investors to participate in projects based on predictable long-term revenue streams

Renewable energy accelerated this trend. Solar and wind projects require significant upfront capital but have very low operating costs once constructed. As a result, project finance structures that emphasize long-term cash flow predictability are particularly well suited for renewable electricity generation.

title: Chapter 11: The Fundamentals of Project Finance for Electricity and Renewable Energy
text:
Understanding the Project Finance Structure
At the heart of project finance is a special purpose vehicle (SPV) — a legally independent entity created solely to develop, own, and operate the project. This entity isolates financial risk from the developer’s broader corporate activities.
The SPV enters a network of contracts that govern the development and operation of the project. These agreements often include:

Power purchase agreements (PPAs)
Engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) contracts
Operations and maintenance (O&M) agreements
Land leases
Interconnection agreements with the electrical grid

Because lenders rely on project cash flows for repayment, these contracts must provide strong assurances that the project will generate reliable revenue over time. The success of a project finance structure therefore depends on contractual certainty and risk allocation across all participants.
